newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Meditation the key to peace in Europe, group says.
newsitem.headline: Meditation the key to peace in Europe, group says.

text.p: Europe's stressed leaders have got it all wrong about bringing peace to the troubled continent. What they and their armies need is meditation, not mediation.
That, at least, is how the Natural Law Party sees things.

In one of the more unusual contributions to the security summit in Lisbon which ended on Tuesday, the party's representatives spent their time lobbying leaders from more than 50 nations to, well, mellow out.

"The conflicts in Ireland, Spain's Basque country and Bosnia, all these conflicts are not ethnic, cultural or religious. It's all down to stress and a lack of consciousness," Reinhard Borowitz, Secretary-General of the council of Natural Law Parties, told a news conference on Tuesday.
"You simply need to move a small number of people practising 'yogic flying' techniques into the area to solve the conflict," he added.
The party said a small group of soldiers practising meditation and yogic flying -- a form of levitation -- rather than using force would help to calm any environment.
"The coherence effect of meditation and 'flying' not only have an effect on each body practising it but also on the environment," said party spokesman John Moore.

The party, which has a presence in 44 countries around the world and runs in elections from the European Union to the United States, says it has scientific proof that the techniques of transcendental meditation are effective peacekeeping tools.
Mozambique adopted meditation towards the end of its recent civil war with hugely successful results, Borowitz said.
"The president trained 15,000 of his troops in meditation and 3,000 in yogic flying and shortly afterwards the fighting stopped," he added.

But the party said that, despite the proof, nations had not been particularly receptive to their ideas at the summit. Moore was shouted down at the closing news conference where he tried to ask heads of state why they had ignored their appeal.
"They're stupid," Borowitz said. "If you took 0.1 percent of foreign aid spent worldwide on funding these groups, you would have peace overnight."
